solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Emma and Kim might be found on this platform (9)

annotation.definition: Emma and Kim might be found on this platform

blocks.note: the surface reads two women's names; the setter means two novels, Jane Austen's Emma and Rudyard Kipling's Kim

blocks.clueFragment: might be found on this platform
blocks.note: not a railway platform or a stage, but any flat surface on which things stand

annotation.surface: Two women, Emma and Kim, are waiting on a railway platform.
annotation.walkthrough: The names read as people and 'platform' as a station; both are book titles, and the platform is where books are kept.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: two famous novels, and the flat surface that holds them, described as a platform.

entries.clue: Way in which one might lead a young filly on? (6,4)

annotation.definition: Way in which one might lead a young filly on?

blocks.note: the surface suggests stringing along a girl, or leading a bride up the aisle; a filly is really a young mare
a way is a track or route, where a horse is led by its headgear

annotation.surface: A man wonders how to string along a young woman.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Filly' is old slang for a young woman, so the clue hints at a bridal path to the altar; the real filly is a horse, led along a riders' track.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: a track for horses, where a young mare might be led on by her bridle, with a sly nod to a bride.

entries.clue: Not all look in a waterway for a coral island (7)

indicatorNotes.Not all: 'not all' of the phrase is wanted, so the answer is a run of letters inside it

blocks.note: lOOK IN A WAterway

annotation.surface: Someone searching a waterway for an island is told not to check all of it.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer spans four words, starting inside 'look' and ending inside 'waterway'.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the Japanese island in the Ryukyu chain is fringed with coral reefs.

entries.clue: Effect of spiked drink with bit of temazepam in it (3,2)

indicatorNotes.spiked: a spiked drink has had a drug slipped into it, and the drug here is E, ecstasy
indicatorNotes.in it: 'in it' means put inside the drink, so T joins E within SUP
indicatorNotes.bit of: a 'bit of' a word is a small piece of it, here its first letter

blocks.note: to sup is to drink
E is ecstasy, the drug that spikes it
first letter of temazepam

annotation.surface: Someone describes what happens after a drink laced with a sleeping pill.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Effect' is a verb here, as in to effect a change, not the noun the surface wants. Two drugs go into the drink: one implied by 'spiked', one named.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as verbs: to effect a plan is to bring it into being, to establish it.

entries.clue: Very loud sleeper might keep this open (3-8)

blocks.note: shrill enough to hurt the ears
a sleeper is a small stud or ring worn to stop a new hole in the lobe closing

annotation.surface: A person snoring loudly might keep their mouth open.
annotation.walkthrough: The sleeper looks like a snorer, but it is a plain earring left in a newly pierced ear to keep the hole open.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: a noise so shrill it seems to pierce the ear, and the hole in the lobe a sleeper earring holds open.

entries.clue: Having lost belly, able to drink a stout (3)

indicatorNotes.Having lost belly: the belly of a word is its middle, so losing it drops the central letter
indicatorNotes.to drink: to drink is to take something inside, so the shortened word takes A into itself

blocks.note: fit to do something is able to do it; minus its middle I, FT
taken inside FT

annotation.surface: A slimmer who has lost their gut can now drink a pint of stout.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stout' looks like the beer being drunk; it is the adjective describing a heavy person.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a stout person is plump and heavily built.

entries.clue: Turn on intro of Pure or Three Lions? (5)

indicatorNotes.intro of: an intro is the opening of a song, so the intro of a word is its first letter
indicatorNotes.on: in an across clue, one part put on another follows it, so RIDE comes after P

blocks.note: first letter of Pure
a turn is a short ride or outing that returns to its start

annotation.surface: A question about the England football anthem Three Lions and a fairground ride.
annotation.walkthrough: Three Lions is the England team's badge and anthem, but the question mark marks it as an example of a group of big cats.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: lions live in family groups with a special collective noun, and three could make a small one.
annotation.definitionNote: Three Lions is an example of the group, hence the question mark.

entries.clue: Spin result, suppressing democratic rigour (9)

indicatorNotes.suppressing: to suppress is to hold something down until it disappears, so D is removed from the word

blocks.note: PR, public relations, is spin
DECISION minus D for democratic

annotation.surface: Political spin produces a result that stifles democratic rigour.
annotation.walkthrough: D is the standard abbreviation for Democrat. 'Spin' and 'democratic' keep the whole clue in politics.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: rigour in argument is exactness and care.

entries.clue: Where one may crash clutching old shades (7)

indicatorNotes.clutching: to clutch is to grip something inside one's hand, so the phrase holds O within it

blocks.note: to crash is slang for sleep; digs are lodgings
O is old

annotation.surface: A car or computer crash while grabbing some old sunglasses.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In digs' is British for living in rented rooms, where one crashes for the night. 'Shades' looks like sunglasses; it means colours.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: these are deep blue-violet colours, and shades are colours.

entries.clue: Accessory of burglar taking judge’s award (4)

indicatorNotes.taking: taking something away from a word leaves the rest, so J is removed

blocks.note: a jemmy is a crowbar for forcing doors
J is the abbreviation for judge, removed

annotation.surface: A judge's prize goes to a burglar's accomplice.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Accessory' reads as an accomplice to the crime; it is the burglar's tool, a jemmy (crowbar in American).
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the American television industry's annual prize is one kind of award.

entries.clue: Your setter would appeal arrests over dope (5)

indicatorNotes.arrests: police who arrest someone hold them in custody, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: I'd: the setter speaking of himself
IT is sex appeal
O is over, in cricket scoring

annotation.surface: The crossword setter plans to appeal against arrests for drugs.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dope' suggests drugs, fitting the arrests; it is a fool. 'Your setter' is the setter's usual way of saying 'I' or 'me'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a dope is a stupid person.

entries.clue: Bounder gets foolish knocking back port (9)

indicatorNotes.knocking back: to knock something back is to push it backwards, so the word is reversed

blocks.note: a bounder and a rotter are both cads
turned round, DAM

annotation.surface: A cad turns silly after downing a glass of port wine.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Knocking back port' looks like drinking the wine; port is the definition, a harbour city. Bounder and rotter are old British words for a cad.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Dutch city is one of Europe's busiest harbours.

entries.clue: Oedipal song in broadcast triggers complaint (4,9)

indicatorNotes.broadcast: to broadcast is originally to scatter seed widely, so the letters are scattered

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 13 letters

annotation.surface: A song about Oedipus on the radio causes listeners to protest.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Complaint' reads as a protest about the song; it is an illness.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: a complaint is an illness, and this one comes from toxic metal building up in the body.

entries.clue: Fruit wrappers a person ripped with glee (6,5)

indicatorNotes.ripped: something ripped is torn to pieces, so the letters are torn up and put back in a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder
anagram fodder

annotation.surface: Someone gleefully tears the wrapping off fruit.
annotation.walkthrough: 'With' simply joins the two sets of letters before the whole lot is ripped up.
annotation.definitionFit: A playful description: citrus skins are nature's wrapping for the fruit inside.

entries.clue: Akin to salt lake and mines scattered around area (6-4)

indicatorNotes.scattered: things scattered are thrown about, so the letters of both words are rearranged
indicatorNotes.around: the rearranged letters go around A, surrounding it

blocks.note: anagram fodder
A is area, enclosed

annotation.surface: A salt lake has minefields spread around it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Salt lake' reads as one thing, but 'salt' belongs to the definition: an old salt is an experienced sailor.
annotation.definitionFit: A crossword staple: a salt is a sailor, so being akin to one means behaving as a sailor does.

entries.clue: Cassius perhaps making love close to Nokia charger (7)

indicatorNotes.making: making one thing into another changes it, so O becomes A
indicatorNotes.close to: the close of a word is its end, so its last letter is taken

blocks.note: Cassius plotted to murder Julius Caesar
O is love, zero in tennis; it goes out
last letter of Nokia, which comes in

annotation.surface: The boxer Cassius Clay makes love near his Nokia phone charger.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Charger' belongs with Nokia as a phone lead, but it is a serving dish. Cassius is not the boxer but the Roman conspirator.
annotation.definitionFit: An old-fashioned synonym: a charger is a large flat dish for serving meat.

entries.clue: Tenor gets musical man out of head on rare port (9)

indicatorNotes.out of head: a person out of their head has lost it, so the name loses its first letter
indicatorNotes.on: in a down clue, one part on another sits below it, so the headless name follows R

blocks.note: T is tenor
R is rare
Stephen Sondheim, the composer of musicals, minus his S

annotation.surface: A tenor gets a musical star drunk on a rare port wine.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Out of head' looks like drunk; it is beheading. Sondheim wrote Sweeney Todd and was a keen cryptic setter himself.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Norwegian city sits on a fjord and is a working harbour.

entries.clue: A personal matter under discussion (2,5)

blocks.note: as printed
the cells a person is made of: matter from a person

annotation.surface: A private affair is being talked about.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Personal matter' reads as a private affair; it is bodily matter, the stuff of a person.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: a question being debated is the one in dispute.

entries.clue: Libyans primarily seen in visit over here! (7)

annotation.definition: Libyans primarily seen in visit over here!

indicatorNotes.primarily: primarily means first of all, so the first letter of Libyans
indicatorNotes.seen in: something seen in a place is inside it, so L goes within the shout

blocks.note: a trip is a visit
a shout to get attention
first letter of Libyans

annotation.surface: An invitation to visit a place full of Libyans.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads straight as an invitation to the Libyan capital while doubling as the wordplay. 'Oi!' is a British shout for attention, much like 'over here!'.
annotation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: the capital of Libya is where a visitor would first meet Libyans.

entries.clue: Where one might see a brother right (2,5)

annotation.definition: Where one might see a brother

blocks.clueFragment: Where one might see a brother
blocks.note: a monk or friar is a brother, living in a religious community
correct, tidy, as it should be

annotation.surface: Someone says a family sighting is about right.
annotation.walkthrough: The first half takes the idiom literally: a brother belongs to a religious community of monks.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: an idiom meaning correct or proper, and the literal place of a friar within his religious body.

entries.clue: Some rejigging ham-fistedly checked material (7)

indicatorNotes.Some: 'some' of the phrase is only part of it, so the answer is a run of letters inside

blocks.note: rejigGING HAM-fistedly

annotation.surface: Someone clumsily reworks a piece of checked fabric.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Checked' reads as inspected; it means patterned in squares.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the cotton cloth is woven in a pattern of small squares.

entries.clue: Hot catch with trapped wind? One’s in shock! (4,3)

indicatorNotes.trapped: something trapped is held inside, so the wind sits within the catch

blocks.note: H is hot, as on a tap
moving air is wind
to net is to catch

annotation.surface: Someone who has eaten something hot is left winded and shocked.
annotation.walkthrough: A shock is a thick mass of hair, not a fright; the exclamation mark flags the pun.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: the mesh worn over the hair sits in a shock, a thick mop of it.
annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a descriptive phrase, not a synonym.

entries.clue: Oscar to appear with piano legends playing benefit (3,3,7)

indicatorNotes.playing: a pianist playing moves across the keys, and the letters of 'piano legends' are moved about

blocks.note: O is Oscar in the NATO alphabet
anagram fodder, 12 letters

annotation.surface: An Oscar winner appears alongside famous pianists at a charity concert.
annotation.walkthrough: Oscar suggests the film award; here it is the NATO code word for its letter. 'Benefit' looks like a charity gig; it is a state payment.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the state payment to the retired is a British welfare benefit.

entries.clue: Toff on revolving stage striking grand’s a dynamite dude (5)

indicatorNotes.on: in a down clue, one part on another sits below it
indicatorNotes.revolving: something revolving turns round, so the letters are turned back to front
indicatorNotes.striking: striking something out deletes it, so G for grand goes

blocks.note: a nob is a toff, an upper-class person
a leg is a stage of a journey; minus G for grand

annotation.surface: A posh man on a revolving stage is a sensational performer.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dynamite dude' reads as slang praise; literally it is the man who invented dynamite. 'Toff' and 'nob' are British for a posh person; G is grand, a thousand.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: the Swedish chemist who invented dynamite and founded the prizes.

entries.clue: Special soldiers sautéed at front for US brass (4)

indicatorNotes.at front: the front of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: the Special Air Service, British special forces
first letter of sautéed

annotation.surface: Special forces are fried up for American top brass.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Brass' looks like military officers, fitting the soldiers; it is British slang for cheek or nerve.
annotation.definitionFit: A regional use: what Britons call brass or cheek, Americans call by this word.

entries.clue: Deal with extremely evasive type getting a talking to? (9)

indicatorNotes.extremely: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so the first and last letters of evasive

blocks.note: to address a problem is to deal with it
the outer letters of evasive

annotation.surface: Handling a slippery character who is being told off.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A talking to' usually means a scolding; the question mark marks the literal sense: someone being spoken to.
annotation.definitionFit: A literal reading: the person a speech or letter is directed at is the one being talked to.

entries.clue: Problem that can come with a load of money (3)

blocks.note: an arithmetic problem set at school
an amount of cash, often a large one

annotation.surface: Wealth brings its own troubles.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a proverb about riches; the problem is a schoolroom one.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: a schoolroom arithmetic exercise, and an amount of money.

entries.clue: Here, gibe not good after black mark given to head (5)

indicatorNotes.not good: a word with 'not good' has lost its G, the abbreviation for good
indicatorNotes.after: coming after something means following it, so these letters follow B

blocks.note: B is black, as on pencils
as in 'the train is in', here
DIG minus G

annotation.surface: A teacher's jibe after giving a head boy a black mark.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Black mark' reads as a reprimand; black is only B, and the mark on the head is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the decorative dot worn on the forehead, especially by Hindu women.

entries.clue: Do one small cocaine hit (5)

blocks.note: S is small, as in clothing sizes
C is slang for cocaine
to ram is to hit

annotation.surface: An order to take a small hit of cocaine.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Do one' is British slang for go away, not an instruction to do a line.
annotation.definitionFit: A slang synonym: both are rude orders to clear off.

entries.clue: A possible producer of a Peck title some knocked (9)

annotation.definition: A possible producer of a Peck

indicatorNotes.knocked: something knocked about is battered out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

annotation.surface: A book by Gregory Peck, or about him, has had some bad reviews.
annotation.walkthrough: The capital P makes Peck look like the actor; a peck is a quick kiss.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: the Christmas plant under which people kiss can produce a quick one.
